what_its_for: Leuprolide is used to treat several conditions. In men, it helps treat prostate cancer by lowering testosterone levels. In women, it treats endometriosis (painful tissue growth outside the uterus), uterine fibroids (noncancerous growths in the uterus), and is used before certain surgeries. It is also used to treat children with precocious puberty (when puberty starts too early, before age 8 in girls or age 9 in boys).
how_to_take: Leuprolide is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a muscle (intramuscular). It comes in different forms: a daily injection you give yourself at home, or a depot (long-acting) injection given by your doctor or nurse every 1, 3, 4, or 6 months. If you are giving the injection yourself at home, your doctor or nurse will show you exactly how to do it. Always rotate the injection site to avoid soreness. Use a new needle each time, and dispose of used needles safely in a sharps container. Do not shake the vial before use. Always wash your hands before preparing your injection.
dosing: The dose and how often you receive it depends on why you are taking leuprolide and which form you are using. Daily injections are typically 1 mg injected under the skin once a day. Depot injections are given every 1, 3, 4, or 6 months depending on the specific product. Your doctor will determine the right dose for you. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you are taking the daily injection and miss a dose, give it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not give two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one. If you miss your scheduled depot injection appointment at your doctor's office, call them right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Missing doses can allow your condition to worsen.
storage: Store unopened vials of leuprolide in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep it away from light. Once mixed (reconstituted), some forms must be used immediately. Check your specific product instructions. Keep all forms of leuprolide out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of used needles and syringes in an approved sharps container — never throw them in the regular trash.
what_to_avoid: Avoid missing doses, as this can allow the condition being treated to come back or worsen. Do not start, stop, or change any other medications without telling your doctor, as some drugs can interact with leuprolide. Women should avoid becoming pregnant while taking leuprolide, as it can harm an unborn baby — use non-hormonal birth control (such as condoms) if needed. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or confused. Avoid alcohol, as it may worsen side effects like hot flashes and dizziness.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: chest pain, sudden numbness or weakness, difficulty breathing, severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat), signs of bone pain that gets suddenly worse, numbness or tingling in arms or legs, trouble urinating or blood in urine, severe depression or thoughts of self-harm, unusual swelling, severe injection site reactions, irregular heartbeat, or vision changes. In children, call the doctor if puberty signs continue or get worse after starting treatment. Women should report any unusual vaginal bleeding.
when_it_works: Leuprolide does not work overnight. For prostate cancer, testosterone levels typically drop to low levels within 2 to 4 weeks. For endometriosis or fibroids, pain and symptoms usually improve within 1 to 3 months of treatment. For precocious puberty in children, signs of early puberty should slow or stop within 1 to 2 months. You may notice some worsening of symptoms in the very first few weeks (called a 'flare') before things start to improve — this is normal. Talk to your doctor if you are not sure whether the medicine is working.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Leuprolide must NOT be used during pregnancy as it can cause miscarriage or harm to the unborn baby. Use effective non-hormonal birth control during treatment. Breastfeeding: It is not known if leuprolide passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Leuprolide is used in children for precocious (early) puberty. Children should be monitored closely by their doctor. Older Adults: Older men being treated for prostate cancer may have a higher risk of bone thinning (osteoporosis), heart problems, and diabetes. Regular monitoring is important. Bone Health: Long-term use can weaken bones in both men and women. Your doctor may recommend calcium, vitamin D, and bone density monitoring.
